q: A municipal shelter plans a TNR campaign to reduce a large closed community cat colony. What minimum percentage of the intact female population must be kept continuously sterilized to stabilize and decrease population size through attrition?
e: Mathematical modeling and population medicine show that a sustained sterilization rate of ≥70% of the intact female population within a geographically locked cohort is required to outpace feline fecundity (1.4 litters/year, ~3 live births/litter). This threshold applies to intact females specifically, not total colony size. Below 70%, the population continues to grow.

q: A municipality proposes replacing TNR with TVHR based on a single modelling study. Which documented real-world disadvantage of TVHR is most important?
o: TVHR eliminates testosterone, causing immediate colony dispersion
TVHR preserves sex hormone production — cats continue nuisance behaviors (fighting, yowling, spraying) and remain at risk for mammary tumours, stump pyometra, and retroviral transmission
TVHR surgeries are faster, creating a shortage of kittens for adoption
TVHR requires lifelong daily progestogens to prevent estrus
e: TVHR preserves gonadal hormone production. Males continue fighting, yowling, and spraying. Females remain at risk for mammary tumours and stump pyometra. Ongoing fighting perpetuates FIV/FeLV transmission. Only ONE modelling study has suggested TVHR superiority — not replicated in field research. TNR remains the evidence-based standard.

q: A veterinary team running a community cat sterilization program wants to minimize trap-shyness. What pre-trapping protocol is evidence-based best practice?
o: Set traps immediately for maximum surprise capture
Place food inside unsecured traps for 2–7 days prior to trapping while withholding all external food sources
Restrict traps to public parks during daylight for safe monitoring
Withhold all food and water for 14 days to maximize bait motivation
e: Acclimatization places food inside unset traps for 2–7 days before active trapping, while withholding food from all other colony feeding stations. This reduces stress, increases trapping efficiency, and reduces trap-shyness in cautious females. Total food/water deprivation for 14 days is inhumane and not recommended.

q: A field biologist describes warehouse cats as 'feral.' Which best defines feral cats in the shelter medicine context?
o: Cats born outdoors that have never received veterinary care
Cats that are untamed and not socialized to humans — defined by socialization level, though this distinction is not consistently applied in published literature
Cats legally classified differently from stray cats in all US jurisdictions
Cats indistinguishable from strays without a minimum 3-day behavioral assessment
e: Feral cats are defined by their socialization level — untamed and not socialized to humans — not by birth location. A kitten born outdoors can become socialized with early handling; an abandoned adult pet retains socialization. This distinction is not consistently applied in published literature, and legal definitions vary by jurisdiction.

q: An unspayed female community cat is identified in a managed colony. What is her estimated maximum lifetime kitten production based on average feline reproductive parameters?
o: 10–20 kittens
20–40 kittens
50–100 kittens
100–200 kittens
e: Female cats are seasonally polyestrous, averaging 1.4 litters per year with 4–5 fetuses per pregnancy (~3 live births per litter). An unspayed female can produce 50–100 kittens in a lifetime. This explains why the ≥70% sterilization threshold is critical — populations rebound rapidly without sustained intervention.

q: A community group proposes relocating a colony of 40 cats from a construction site to a public park. Which statement best reflects the shelter medicine position on trap-neuter-relocate?
o: Relocation is preferred for all displaced colonies
Relocation is not routinely recommended — it is challenging, expensive, and newly relocated cats often attempt to return if not confined during transition
Relocation is only acceptable if cats are adopted out within 90 days
Relocation is legally prohibited in all US states
e: Trap-neuter-relocate is not routinely recommended due to time, expense, and logistical challenges. Suitable sites require reliable food, shelter, and a caretaker. Failure to confine newly relocated cats during the transition results in attempts to return to the original colony location. Relocation may be necessary when cats' safety is at risk or severe ecological concerns exist.

q: A welfare assessment is conducted in a community cat colony. Which combination of parameters constitutes the evidence-based visual welfare scale for free-roaming cats?
o: Weight, body temperature, respiratory rate, mucosal color
BCS, coat condition, nasal/ocular discharge, ear crusting, and visible injuries
Fecal consistency, coat condition, mobility, hydration
Microchip status, vaccination record, dental score, behavior assessment
e: The validated visual welfare scale for community cats assesses: BCS, coat condition, nasal/ocular discharge, ear crusting, and visible injuries. All parameters can be assessed without physical handling — making them practical for field assessment of free-roaming populations.

q: Which management approach for free-roaming cats is most strongly associated with rapid population rebound (the 'vacuum effect')?
o: TNR with <70% sterilization of intact females
Trap-remove-euthanize programs that fail to fully eliminate all cats from an area
TVHR programs where hormone production is maintained
Sanctuary placement programs
e: TRE programs that do not achieve complete removal of all cats from an area — and do not prevent immigration — rapidly repopulate through the vacuum effect. Remaining reproductive individuals and immigrating cats from surrounding areas fill the cleared territory. TNR reduces this by maintaining sterilized territorial residents that deter new arrivals.

q: Which published finding about disease prevalence in free-roaming community cats is most relevant for policy discussions?
o: Free-roaming cats have significantly higher infectious disease rates, representing a greater zoonotic reservoir
Infectious and parasitic infection rates in free-roaming cats are similar to owned cats — they do not represent a greater public health reservoir
Free-roaming cats have no infectious disease risk due to natural selection
Free-roaming cats have lower disease rates due to herd immunity within colonies
e: Published studies show infectious disease and parasitic infection rates in free-roaming cats are similar to owned cats. Free-roaming cats do not pose a greater zoonotic risk than owned cats and do not serve as unique disease reservoirs. This is a critical finding for evidence-based community cat management policy discussions.

q: A TNR program is achieving 50% sterilization of the intact female population in a large open colony. What is the expected population trend?
o: Population will slowly stabilize over 5–10 years
Population will decline proportional to sterilization achieved
Population will continue to grow — 50% does not meet the ≥70% threshold needed to outpace feline fecundity
Population will collapse due to reduced kitten survival
e: A 50% sterilization rate is insufficient. The ≥70% threshold of intact females must be achieved AND maintained within a geographically locked cohort to outpace feline reproductive capacity. At 50%, feline fecundity exceeds the impact of sterilization and the population continues to grow despite the program.

q: A public survey on community cat management is conducted. Which finding is most consistent with published literature?
o: The majority of the public support lethal control as the most humane and effective strategy
Euthanasia is the most publicly acceptable management option
The overwhelming majority prefer leaving free-roaming cats outdoors over euthanasia, even knowing a cat could die of traumatic injury within 2 years
Most people are indifferent to free-roaming cat welfare
e: Published surveys consistently show the overwhelming majority prefer leaving free-roaming cats outdoors over capture and euthanasia — even when informed that outdoor life involves trauma and death within 2 years. Euthanasia is identified as the LEAST acceptable management option. No management strategy succeeds at large scale without public cooperation.

q: Why should observed colony size reductions in TVHR studies be interpreted cautiously?
o: Colony size reductions are entirely explained by successful sterilization of females
Observed reductions may reflect decreased lifespan in hormonally intact animals (from fighting, mammary tumours, reproductive pathologies) rather than strategic population control efficacy
TVHR produces stronger FIV/FeLV immunity, explaining improved survival
TVHR reduces immigration more effectively than TNR, explaining population reduction
e: Colony size reductions in TVHR studies require cautious interpretation — they may reflect the decreased lifespan of cats retaining their gonads (injuries from fighting, mammary neoplasia, reproductive pathologies) rather than positive population control. True strategic efficacy would require demonstrating comparable or superior reduction to TNR through attrition over time, which has not been demonstrated in field research.

q: A shelter is preparing to adopt out a dog with a documented history of mild resource-guarding bites to two previous owners. What is the shelter's mandatory disclosure obligation under ASV Guidelines?
o: Disclosure is optional if the adopter appears experienced with dogs
All known bite incidents must be documented in hardcopy or electronic form and provided to the adopter — verbal disclosure alone is insufficient
The shelter may withhold bite history if the dog has been behaviour-assessed and cleared as 'low risk'
Disclosure is only required if the bites resulted in medical treatment
e: ASV Guidelines require that a record of ALL known bite incidents be documented in hardcopy or electronic form and provided to adopters, fosters, and transfer partners. This is a non-negotiable disclosure obligation regardless of bite severity or behaviour assessment outcome. Verbal disclosure alone is not sufficient — written documentation must be transferred with the animal.

q: A shelter staff member is bitten on the forearm by a stray dog. The bite breaks the skin. What is the correct immediate wound management sequence?
o: Apply a tourniquet, then seek medical attention
Immediately wash with soap and antiseptic (e.g., povidone-iodine), irrigate under pressure with saline via 20 mL syringe and 18G needle, cover, and seek medical attention
Apply a pressure bandage only — irrigation is not recommended for deep punctures
No immediate treatment needed; seek medical attention only if swelling develops within 24 hours
e: Immediate bite wound management: (1) wash thoroughly with soap and antiseptic with virucidal activity (povidone-iodine preferred); (2) irrigate under pressure using a 20 mL syringe and 18G needle with saline; (3) cover the wound; (4) seek medical attention. Immediate washing significantly reduces infection risk. If the hand is bitten, elevate it. Do not delay treatment.

q: A city council is considering passing breed-specific legislation (BSL) banning pit bull-type dogs within the municipality, citing public safety concerns. Which statement best represents the position of the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA)?
o: BSL is effective when combined with owner education programs and should be selectively supported
BSL is not effective at reducing dog bite incidence; the AVMA opposes it in favour of individual behaviour-based assessment and responsible ownership ordinances
BSL is supported by the AVMA as a last resort when dangerous dog laws have failed
BSL is acceptable for use in shelters but not in private residences
e: The AVMA, along with ASV and most major veterinary organisations, opposes BSL because it is not supported by evidence as effective for reducing dog bite incidence. BSL targets breed/appearance rather than individual animal behaviour, owner responsibility, or situational factors. Evidence-based alternatives include individual dangerous dog laws, owner education, bite prevention programs, and enforcement of responsible ownership ordinances.

q: A stray dog bites a child at a park and is impounded by animal control. The dog appears healthy on intake. On day 8 of the mandatory observation period, the dog escapes and is hit by a vehicle, dying at the scene. What must happen?
o: The dog may be cremated — it showed no clinical signs of rabies and died from trauma, not disease
The dog's head must be cooled (not frozen) and shipped to an approved diagnostic laboratory for mandatory rabies testing — any death during the 10-day observation window requires testing
The 10-day clock resets when a new biting incident occurs
Rabies testing is only required if the dog displayed neurological signs before death
e: Any dog, cat, or ferret that bites a human and dies for ANY reason within the mandatory 10-day observation window requires rabies testing. This includes accidental death from trauma. The head must be cooled (not frozen) — freezing and thawing destroys brain tissue architecture, potentially rendering the gold-standard dFA test unreadable. Public health law makes this testing mandatory regardless of the cause of death.

q: According to the Dunbar bite severity scale, which level describes a bite where at least one puncture is deeper than half the length of the canine tooth, possibly with deep bruising or bidirectional lacerations from head-shaking?
o: Level 2 — skin contact but no puncture
Level 3 — puncture(s) present but none deeper than half the canine tooth length
Level 4 — at least one puncture deeper than half the canine tooth; dog did not self-inhibit
Level 5 — multiple Level 4 bites in a single incident
e: Level 4 on the Dunbar scale describes 1–4 punctures where at least one exceeds half the canine tooth length, often with deep bruising or bidirectional lacerations from the dog holding and shaking. This indicates the dog applied sustained pressure and failed to self-inhibit — a qualitatively different risk from Level 3 (all punctures shallower than half tooth depth). Level 4+ bites are the threshold at which most shelter protocols significantly restrict or preclude public adoption without specialist behaviour evaluation.

q: A shelter dog has a documented history of a single Level 2 Dunbar bite. Which statement best characterises what a Level 2 bite means?
o: Level 2 requires immediate euthanasia under most shelter safety protocols
The dog made skin contact without puncturing the skin — Level 2 bites are generally manageable with behaviour modification and trigger avoidance
Level 2 is the threshold for restricted public adoption — equivalent to a Level 4 clinical risk
Level 2 means no skin contact occurred; the dog snapped without touching the victim
e: Level 2 on the Dunbar scale describes skin contact without puncture — redness, bruising, or surface abrasions may occur but the skin is not broken. This is generally considered manageable with behaviour modification and careful management of identified bite contexts. Level 1 (no skin contact at all) and Level 2 are the lowest-risk bite categories. The critical question in every Level 2 case is the bite context, frequency, and predictability — not the level alone.

q: Which of the following is the strongest individual animal risk factor for dog bite incidents based on epidemiological data?
o: Body weight greater than 30 kg (66.1 lb)
Intact male status
Positive kennel cough history
History of shelter housing for more than 14 days
e: Intact male dogs have a significantly higher bite rate than neutered males — this is one of the most consistently replicated individual animal risk factors across multiple bite epidemiology studies. Testosterone-driven territorial, competitive, and inter-male aggression contributes to this difference. Neuter status is therefore a core component of bite prevention messaging, though neutering alone does not eliminate bite risk from fear, pain, or resource guarding behaviours.

q: Which two groups are at highest risk of serious injury or death from dog bites in US epidemiological data, and why are children at elevated facial bite risk?
o: Adult males 18–35 and animal control officers — due to daily occupational exposure
Veterinary staff and postal workers — due to frequency of bite incidents
Children under 5 and the elderly; children's height positions their face and neck at dog-head level and they cannot read canine warning signals
Pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals — due to impaired wound healing and infection risk
e: Children under 5 and the elderly are the groups at highest risk for serious injury or death from dog bites. Children are particularly at risk for facial and neck injuries because their height positions these structures at the same level as a medium or large dog's head. They also lack the developmental capacity to recognise and respond appropriately to canine warning signals (stiffening, growling, lip curl, whale eye). The elderly face increased risk due to slower reflexes and reduced physical resilience. The majority of bites in both groups involve familiar dogs, not random stranger attacks.

q: What is the purpose of ear-tipping in a TNR programme, and which ear is the universal convention?
o: Ear-tipping is a temporary marker removed at subsequent trapping; either ear can be used depending on local protocol

Ear-tipping (surgical removal of the distal ~1 cm of the left ear tip under anaesthesia) is a permanent, universally recognisable field identifier indicating the cat has been sterilised, vaccinated, and returned — it prevents unnecessary re-trapping and repeated anaesthesia
Ear-tipping is applied only to cats confirmed FIV-negative and serves as a serological record
Ear-tipping is an alternative to microchipping for cats that cannot be scanned
e: Ear-tipping — surgical removal of approximately 1/4 inch (about 1 cm) of the tip of the left ear under anaesthesia during the TNR procedure — is the universally accepted permanent field identifier for community cats that have been sterilised, vaccinated, and returned. It is visible at a distance without handling, allowing animal control officers, shelter staff, and caretakers to identify already-processed cats and avoid re-trapping. The convention is the LEFT ear. Ear-tipping does not replace microchipping but is the primary identification tool in the field.

q: According to NASPHV guidelines, what is the recommended rabies vaccination protocol for cats in a TNR programme, and what does even a single vaccination provide?
o: A single vaccination provides no clinically meaningful protection — cats require a full 3-dose primary series before release

Cats should receive a licensed 3-year rabies vaccine at TNR, be re-trapped for a booster at 1 year, then every 3 years; even one injection provides significant public health benefit as feral cats mount adequate antibody responses
Cats should receive only a 1-year killed vaccine annually — 3-year products are contraindicated in feral populations
Rabies vaccination is not required in TNR because feral cats are not classified as domestic animals under federal rabies law
e: NASPHV guidelines recommend vaccinating all TNR cats with a licensed 3-year rabies vaccine. The re-trapping schedule calls for a booster at 1 year, then every 3 years thereafter. Critically, even a single immunisation provides significant public health benefit — studies confirm that feral cats mount adequate antibody responses to a single rabies injection, increasing herd immunity within the free-roaming cat population. Rabies vaccination during TNR is one of the programme's core public health contributions.

q: Two separate studies have measured the post-return death rate for cats returned to their capture site following TNR. What is this rate, and what does it imply about community cat welfare?
o: Approximately 30% of returned cats die within 1 year
Approximately 6% confirmed death rate post-return; cats surviving to adulthood are expected to do well for several years or longer
Approximately 50% die within 6 months from vehicle trauma and predation
No peer-reviewed data on post-return mortality exist — this is a known evidence gap
e: Two separate published studies confirmed a post-return death rate of approximately 6% following TNR and return to the capture site. Cats that survive the initial post-return period and reach adulthood are expected to do well for several years or longer. Human feeding is consistently associated with improved survival and longer lifespans in managed colonies. Sterilisation further improves health by reducing pyometra, mammary tumours, and fighting-related FIV transmission. The 6% figure is critical for rebutting the argument that any outdoor cat life is uniformly poor welfare.

q: A shelter implements a Return-to-Field (RTF) programme, sterilising impounded stray cats and returning them to their community. Which statement best characterises RTF as a standalone intervention?
o: RTF is the most evidence-based standalone method for reducing community cat populations
RTF independently achieves population reduction comparable to TNR within 18 months

RTF does not independently reduce cat populations and may be legally problematic in some jurisdictions; it should be used in combination with established TNR infrastructure, not as a standalone programme
RTF is equivalent to TNR and interchangeable for programme planning purposes
e: Return-to-Field (RTF) — also called Shelter-Neuter-Return (SNR) — diverts impounded stray cats from shelter housing and euthanasia through sterilisation and community return. However, it does not independently reduce community cat populations without accompanying TNR infrastructure already in place. Some jurisdictions have legal concerns about returning impounded animals. RTF's documented benefits are reducing shelter intake burden and preventing euthanasia of impounded cats; it contributes to sterilisation coverage when combined with active TNR, but it is not a substitute for a comprehensive programme.
